page3_img_1.png.title: Three-stage research method for studying code review comment usefulness
page3_img_1.png.description: A left-to-right flow diagram showing the paper’s three-stage methodology. Stage 1 (Exploratory Study) depicts developer interviews that produce "comments rated by interviewees" and a list of “characteristics of useful comments.” Stage 2 (Building an Automated Classifier) shows manual classification of comments feeding into a dataset of useful comments (the oracle), extraction of signals/attributes, and a build/validate step that produces an automated classifier (represented by interlocking gears). Stage 3 (Empirical Study) shows the classifier being applied to five projects to generate charts and graphs for analysis. The visual emphasizes the iterative hand-off: interview findings inform manual labeling and signal selection, which are used to train and validate the classifier that is then scaled to large-scale empirical analysis.

page7_img_1.png.title: Keywords associated with Useful vs Not Useful code review comments
page7_img_1.png.description: A two-column table listing words that are statistically more frequent in comments labeled ‘Useful’ (left) versus ‘Not Useful’ (right). Useful examples include command and corrective terms such as "assert", "fix", "remove", "move", and polite requests like "please" and "should"; Not Useful examples include question/acknowledgement words such as "why", "how", "which", "yes", "already", and negations like "not"/"doesn’t". The paper notes these keywords were drawn from terms appearing in at least 15 comments and that each listed word was at least twice as likely to appear in one class than the other, supporting the authors’ observation that imperative/requesting language correlates with useful feedback while questions and acknowledgements correlate with less useful comments.

page9_img_1.png.title: Usefulness density by team membership and temporal trends (Office, Bing)
page9_img_1.png.description: The figure combines a small table (Table III) and two temporal line charts. The table reports comment usefulness density when the reviewer and author are on the same team versus different teams for five projects: Azure (Yes 68.0%, No 69.4%), Bing (Yes 67.8%, No 68.6%), Visual Studio (Yes 66.0%, No 69.1%), Exchange (Yes 62.5%, No 63.7%), and Office (Yes 66.7%, No 66.9%) — differences between same-team and cross-team reviewers are very small (under ~1.5%). The Office time-series (panel a) shows an overall upward trend in usefulness density with fluctuations and a peak near 72.5% toward the end of the sampled periods (dashed red trendline slopes upward). The Bing time-series (panel b) shows a decline from the mid-60s to a low near 61% in the middle periods, followed by a recovery back to roughly the mid-60s by the end of the series.

page8_img_2.png.title: Usefulness density vs. reviewers' prior reviews in the file
page8_img_2.png.description: Line chart showing how the proportion of useful review comments (Usefulness Density, y-axis 35%–80%) varies with a reviewer’s number of prior reviews of the same file (x-axis 0–20). Five projects are plotted (Azure: red circles; Bing: blue triangles; Exchange: green squares; Office: purple crosses; Visual Studio: orange diamonds). All projects show a large jump from ~32–37% usefulness for first-time reviewers (x=0) to roughly 65–71% after one prior review, followed by a modest increase over the next few reviews and a plateau around ~70–80% after about five prior reviews; Exchange consistently remains lower than the others (≈65–68%). This supports the paper’s finding that prior review experience on a file substantially increases the density of useful comments, with diminishing returns after several reviews.

page8_img_1.png.title: Decision tree for classifying review comments as useful or not useful
page8_img_1.png.description: A flow-chart decision tree showing the model used to classify a review comment as Useful (green rounded boxes) or Not Useful (brown rounded boxes). The root question (top diamond) asks: “Is there any change within one line of the comment-highlighted lines in any of the subsequent iterations?” If Yes, the tree next asks whether the thread status is “Won’t fix” (Yes → Not Useful; No → Useful). If No at the root, the tree again checks thread status “Won’t fix”; if that is No it asks whether there is only one comment in the thread (Yes → branch that tests iteration number > 2 and thread status Closed to decide Useful vs Not Useful; No → branch that tests whether the thread sentiment is “Strongly Positive” to decide Useful vs Not Useful). The diagram therefore highlights ChangeTrigger (one-line proximity), thread status, number of comments, iteration number, and sentiment as the key attributes driving the Useful/Not Useful classification.

page6_img_1.png.title: Detecting change-triggering review comments across iterations
page6_img_1.png.description: Two side-by-side example panels illustrating how the authors detect whether a review comment triggered a code change by comparing iterations. Panel (a) shows a code excerpt (lines ~51–63) with reviewer-highlighted regions (red/yellow) and a comment popup (status “Closed”) while the corresponding change in a later iteration appears three lines away; panel (b) shows two comment popups in very close proximity and an “Iteration 1” popup indicating threaded discussion. The small vertical proximity glyph between panels (green/red markers) visually encodes where changes occurred relative to comment locations and motivates the paper’s decision to treat changes within one line of a comment as a reliable “change trigger” to reduce false positives/negatives when changes occur farther away or when multiple nearby comments exist.

page7_img_2.png.title: Comment usefulness density by project
page7_img_2.png.description: A table summarizing review activity and usefulness for five Microsoft projects (Azure — cloud software; Bing — search engine; Visual Studio — development tools; Exchange — email server; Office — office suite). It lists number of reviews, total comments, number of comments classified as useful, and the resulting usefulness density for each project. Across all projects there are 190,050 reviews and 1,496,340 comments, of which 979,440 were classified useful for an overall usefulness density of 65.5%. Per-project usefulness densities range from 63.3% (Exchange) to 68.6% (Azure); Azure and Office show the highest densities (68.6% and 68.0%), while Bing (64.2%) and Exchange (63.3%) have the lowest, with Bing contributing the largest volume of reviews and comments (92,987 reviews, 664,619 comments).

page9_img_2.png.title: Usefulness density vs. changeset size across five Microsoft projects
page9_img_2.png.description: Line chart showing the proportion of review comments classified as useful (y-axis, percent) by number of files in the changeset (x-axis, 1–40) for five projects: Azure (red circles), Bing (blue triangles), Exchange (green squares), Office (purple pluses), and Visual Studio (orange Xs). All projects begin near the mid-to-high 60% range for very small changesets, and most show a general decline in usefulness density as the number of files increases; Exchange stays lowest (around ~60–66%), Azure and Office are typically highest (~67–73%), Bing is relatively stable (~62–66%), and Visual Studio is the most volatile with occasional dips below 60%. This visual confirms the paper’s empirical finding that larger changesets tend to elicit a lower proportion of useful comments and highlights project-specific variation in that effect.

page3_img_2.png.title: Stacked distribution of review comment categories by usefulness
page3_img_2.png.description: A stacked bar chart (y-axis = percentage of overall comments) showing 13 comment categories on the x-axis (1: Documentation, 2: Visual Representation, 3: Organization, 4: Solution Approach, 5: Resource, 6: Validation, 7: Logical, 8: Synchronization, 9: Supporting library, 10: Defect, 11: API calls, 12: False Positive, 13: Other). Each bar is split into three usefulness classes (Not Useful — pale yellow, Somewhat Useful — teal, Useful — blue). Comments that map to functional defect categories (roughly categories 5–11) are dominated by the blue Useful segments, while the first four categories (documentation, visual, organization, solution approach — the ‘‘evolvability’’ issues) contain a larger share of Somewhat Useful responses. Not Useful ratings are concentrated in the False Positive and Other categories; overall the interviewees judged almost 69% of comments to be Useful or Somewhat Useful.

page2_img_1.png.title: CodeFlow review UI showing inline diff, file/reviewer panes, and an overlaid comment thread
page2_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of the CodeFlow review interface with labeled panes: a left file list, a central diff view (C) showing highlighted lines in a source file, a reviewer/status pane (B), a comment-summary area (D) and iteration tabs across the top (E). An inline comment popup is overlaid on the diff (F), attached to exception-handling lines in the file and asking an actionable question about error-flushing behavior; the popup displays participant responses, a status selector (e.g., Closed), and a control to hide the thread. The bottom pane shows the threaded conversation history for the file and the left pane lists other files in the change, illustrating the multi-iteration review workflow and how comments are tied to specific lines — the exact UI elements the paper used to derive features such as comment status, participant counts, and proximity-based change triggers for the usefulness classifier.
